title: Bayes-Sufficient Compression Is Not Enough: How Does Communication Help Multi-Agent Systems?
claim: Two messages can both carry the information needed for the right action, yet only the concise one is usable by the receiver.
layout: 2 stacked rows, chat reply left with illustration right, top-to-bottom, ≠ caption
description: A chat-style cartoon built around one question. A User bubble at the top asks, "It's raining. I'm going outside. Should I take an umbrella?" Below are two rows, each pairing a reply card with an illustration. The top row is a "GPT Pro" reply: a long, formal paragraph that never gets to the point. It has a green "Correct & Bayes-sufficient" banner. Beside it, a worried man in a yellow sweater scratches his head over his phone, with a red question mark and the thought bubble "So... should I take it?" The bottom row is a "GPT" reply in large bold text, "Yes. Take an umbrella.", with the same green banner. Beside it, the same man smiles under an umbrella in the rain, with a green checkmark. A bold caption at the bottom reads "Bayes-sufficient ≠ receiver-usable". The eye goes first to the large bold short reply and the two contrasting faces.
caption: Bayes-sufficient is not the same as receiver-usable. Illustrative example, constructed for exposition rather than taken from model logs. Both replies are correct and Bayes-sufficient: each carries the information that determines the right action. The verbose reply leaves the user unsure what to do, whereas the short reply leads directly to the action. The framework attributes this difference to the receiver’s bounded decoder and the protocol tax of the message (Section 2); Theorem 3 shows that Bayes sufficiency alone does not make a message receiver-optimal.
abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems pair a sender with broad context and an executor with a limited local view. We study when a short message improves the executor's next decision, when raw context is preferable, and when a stronger sender helps. Our framework, \emph{receiver-relative bounded coordination}, expresses message utility as receiver gain minus protocol tax. Compression beats raw context when tax savings exceed losses from omitted information and decoder mismatch. Even \emph{Bayes-sufficient} compression can fail when a bounded executor cannot use its surface form. A three-stage decomposition separates externalization, absorption, and \emph{action closure}, explaining how errors remain after the correct content reaches the receiver. Under a single-crossing condition, sender upgrades help above a receiver-burden threshold. Across six benchmarks, the same Qwen protocol raises ContextBench joint accuracy from $0.633$ to $0.775$ but lowers ToolSandbox from $0.889$ to $0.653$. Fixed-message replay reveals closure failures despite correct artifact recovery. These results guide an inference-time selector that improves the accuracy-cost frontier on the evaluated communication regimes.
